assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Vein
items.clue: A vessel that carries blood back towards the heart at low pressure.

items.label: Lignin
items.clue: A hard, waterproof polymer deposited in the walls of xylem vessels.

items.label: Transpiration
items.clue: The loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves.

items.label: Correlation coefficient
items.clue: A number between -1 and +1 that quantifies how strongly two variables are related.

questions.stem: Why does gas exchange become a greater challenge as organisms increase in size?

options.text: The surface area-to-volume ratio decreases, and the distance from the centre of the organism to its exterior increases.
The surface area-to-volume ratio increases, so far more gas has to cross each unit of the exchange surface.
Only animals with lungs or gills exchange gases, so the challenge arises once an organism is big enough to have them.
A large organism uses more oxygen in total; the distance gases must diffuse to reach its cells makes no difference.

questions.stem: Why is the surface of a gas-exchange organ kept moist?

options.text: The moisture is not needed for exchange; it only keeps the cells of the surface from drying out and dying.
The moisture forms a sticky layer that traps dust and pathogens before they reach the exchange surface.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in the film of water before diffusing across the cell membranes.
The water is absorbed into the blood across the surface, carrying the dissolved oxygen in with it.

questions.stem: What is the function of surfactant in the alveoli of a mammalian lung?

options.text: It traps dust and microorganisms in a sticky layer so that they can be swept out of the lungs.
It lowers the surface tension of the moisture lining the alveoli, so they do not collapse and inflate easily.
It is the film of water absorbed into the blood, carrying the oxygen dissolved in it across the alveolar wall.
It dries the alveolar lining so that gases cross the wall as gases rather than having to dissolve first.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events draws air into the lungs during inspiration?

options.text: Air entering the lungs inflates them, and the inflating lungs push the ribs outward and the diaphragm downward.
The muscular walls of the lungs contract, widening the alveoli and sucking air in through the trachea.
The diaphragm relaxes and rises into a dome, and the ribs move up so that air is drawn in to fill the space.
The diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thorax volume rises and lung pressure falls.

questions.stem: A student's spirometer readings are: tidal volume 0.5 dm³, inspiratory reserve volume 3.0 dm³, expiratory reserve volume 1.2 dm³. What is the student's vital capacity?

options.text: 4.2 dm³
4.7 dm³
3.5 dm³
1.7 dm³

questions.explanation: Vital capacity is the maximum volume that can be exhaled after the deepest inhalation, which is tidal volume + inspiratory reserve + expiratory reserve = 0.5 + 3.0 + 1.2 = 4.7 dm³.

questions.stem: What causes a stoma to open?

options.text: The guard cells take up water and swell, and their unevenly thickened walls make them bend apart.
The guard cells contract like muscle cells, pulling the two edges of the pore apart from one another.
The guard cells lose water and shrink, leaving a gap between them through which the gases can pass.
The plant needs to lose water to pull the transpiration stream up the xylem, and that need triggers opening.

questions.stem: Which statement about a plan diagram of a transverse section of a dicotyledonous leaf is correct?

options.text: It shows a few representative cells of each tissue in outline, including their nuclei and chloroplasts.
It shows the outline and position of each tissue, with the palisade mesophyll directly beneath the upper epidermis.
It shows each vein with phloem above the xylem, because the phloem lies nearer to the upper surface.
It shows the spongy mesophyll directly beneath the upper epidermis, above the palisade mesophyll.

questions.stem: A student counts the stomata visible in five different fields of view on the lower epidermis of a leaf: 22, 26, 19, 27 and 21. The area of one field of view at high power is 0.20 mm². What is the stomatal density?

options.text: 115 per mm²
575 per mm²
110 per mm²
4.6 per mm²

questions.stem: Why is the wall of a capillary only one cell thick?

options.text: It keeps the distance over which substances diffuse between blood and tissue cells very short.
It lets blood pass through the capillary faster, so that more blood reaches the tissue cells.
It leaves room for a lumen wide enough for red blood cells to pass through side by side.
It allows red blood cells to squeeze out through the wall and into the tissues.

questions.explanation: Exchange across the capillary wall is by diffusion, and the rate of diffusion falls steeply as distance increases. A wall of a single endothelial cell keeps that distance to a minimum, so exchange is rapid.

questions.stem: The pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Which statement about this vessel is correct?

options.text: It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, whatever the oxygen content.
It carries oxygenated blood, because by definition every artery carries oxygenated blood.
Its wall is thick and rigid so that pressure from the right ventricle cannot burst it.
Its muscular wall contracts to pump the deoxygenated blood along to the lungs.

questions.stem: Why can heart rate be determined by feeling the carotid or radial pulse with the fingertips?

options.text: Because blood is pushed past the fingertips in one surge each time the muscular artery wall contracts.
Because the blood flowing through the artery can be felt as it moves past the fingertips.
Because a pressure wave passes along the artery wall each time the left ventricle contracts.
Because these are the places where large veins close to the surface of the skin carry the heartbeat.

questions.stem: Which combination of features adapts a vein for returning blood to the heart at low pressure?

options.text: A thick layer of muscle that contracts rhythmically, and a narrow lumen that keeps the pressure high.
Valves that open and shut actively to push blood along, and a wall of elastic tissue that recoils.
A pulse that travels along the wall and squeezes blood forwards, and a thick wall to resist it.
Valves that prevent backflow, and a flexible wall compressed by surrounding muscle.
